question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Indian handicraft/industry centres that suffered deindustrialization under British rule]
options: Dhaka (Dacca) — Famous for Muslin weaving; industry collapsed due to cheap British mill cloth
Murshidabad — Erstwhile capital of Bengal; silk weaving declined sharply after Company control
Surat — Declined as a textile and shipbuilding port after Bombay became the British headquarters
Ahmedabad — Completely deindustrialized in the 18th century with no textile survival into the 19th century
wrong_fact: Ahmedabad was NOT completely deindustrialized; it retained a significant handloom textile tradition and later became a centre of Indian-owned modern cotton mills in the late 19th century, earning the name 'Manchester of India'.
explanation: Dhaka's famous Muslin declined catastrophically under British rule. Murshidabad silk suffered as Company revenues replaced Nawab patronage. Surat declined relative to Bombay. However, Ahmedabad is the odd one out — it actually survived deindustrialization pressures and went on to industrialize under Indian entrepreneurs, becoming a major cotton mill centre by the 1860s–1880s.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Craft/industry and the region most associated with its British-era decline]
options: Wootz steel production — Mainly centred in Hyderabad and Mysore regions; declined after cheap British iron imports
Bidri metalwork — Bidar (Karnataka); largely survived because it catered to luxury niche markets
Patola silk weaving — Patan, Gujarat; declined significantly due to British import of French silk
Shipbuilding — Surat and Masulipatnam; declined after British Navigation Acts restricted Indian-built ships
wrong_fact: Patola silk in Patan, Gujarat, declined due to reduced royal patronage and economic pressure, but its primary competitor was NOT French silk imports — rather, it was cheaper machine-made imitation textiles and reduced court patronage; Patola weavers also emigrated to avoid penury.
explanation: Wootz steel from the Deccan (Hyderabad-Mysore belt) was undercut by cheap British iron/steel. Bidri metalwork from Bidar survived as a luxury craft. Indian shipbuilding at Surat and Masulipatnam was hobbled by British Navigation Acts. Patola silk did decline, but attributing it specifically to 'French silk imports' is incorrect — competition came from cheaper machine-made textiles and loss of aristocratic patronage, not primarily from French imports.

question: Which of the following is NOT correctly matched? [Historian/economist and their specific geographic/thematic analysis of deindustrialization]
options: Amiya Kumar Bagchi — Quantified weavers' decline in Gangetic Bihar using 1809–1813 and 1901 census comparisons
R.C. Dutt — Documented destruction of Bengal's cotton weaving through selective import duties favouring British cloth
D.R. Gadgil — Analysed industrial regression in western India (Deccan) in 'Industrial Evolution of India'
Morris D. Morris — Argued deindustrialization was most severe in Madras Presidency relative to Bengal and Bombay
wrong_fact: Morris D. Morris did NOT argue deindustrialization was most severe in Madras relative to Bengal and Bombay. Morris famously contested the deindustrialization thesis itself, arguing the evidence was ambiguous and that real wages may not have fallen uniformly — he did not single out Madras as the most severely affected region.
explanation: Bagchi's statistical work on Bihar weavers is well-established. R.C. Dutt's work on Bengal is foundational. D.R. Gadgil studied western India's industrial evolution. Morris D. Morris was actually a revisionist who questioned the extent of deindustrialization rather than identifying Madras as its epicentre. Attributing a Madras-centric severity argument to Morris is historically inaccurate.
